raw.assessment: The incumbent combines selection, removable assembly, order checking and a layout diagram, plausibly reducing customer construction work while retaining rearrangeability. Performance misses the time target (11-minute median); seven of ten observed customers succeeded unaided. Five reported partition problems warrant investigation but do not establish five verified packing errors. Repeated three-compartment orders taking seven to nine minutes support retaining the basic process; mixed batches containing every extreme delay suggest switching or complexity, without separating them. A concrete limit on a dimensional explanation is D2-O5: measured widths overlap between successful and retried insertions, so width alone is not an established cause. Neither proposed opening establishes pilot success.

openings.claim: Order-specific staging and a component tally may reduce searching, selection errors and repeated checking in mixed-layout work.
openings.delta: Add a reusable staging area keyed to the accepted layout and exterior color before the existing insertion and packing steps.
openings.prediction: Compared with the incumbent, matched mixed orders show less selection/checking time and fewer verified component discrepancies; unchanged insertion time would localize the benefit.
openings.probe: Use six reusable sample sets within the 15-sample allowance. Alternate baseline and staged runs across workers, balancing layout and color. Time each stage, including staging, and independently reconcile packed components against the order. Compare identical layouts across methods.
assumptions: Measured preparation and trial time fit the fixed delivery schedule.
Initial spending stays at most 500 and recurring material increase at most 0.40 per order.

openings.claim: Some customer difficulty may come from mapping the short partition to the ordered layout even when the supplied parts are correct.
openings.delta: Replace the generic three-layout diagram with an order-specific diagram identifying the short partition and its slot.
openings.prediction: With verified identical contents, the specific diagram reduces short-partition placement errors and requests for help.
openings.probe: Allocate the ten participants evenly between diagrams, balancing ordered layouts. Record unaided completion, placement errors and time. Treat results as directional evidence, not proof of the 90% pilot target.
assumptions: Participants can test without prior exposure to the alternative diagram.
Diagram preparation and printing fit the remaining shared budget and delivery time.
Product geometry, removable joints, assortment, accepted counts and colors remain unchanged.

raw.assessment: Selection, interpretation and insertion bottlenecks are plausible; combined timing cannot establish their contributions. Neither opening is demonstrated. Adoption requires measured costs, timing and customer outcomes within the fixed delivery date.

openings.claim: Hypothesis: make each order a temporary spatial kit. Use reusable board silhouettes for required partitions; assemble after every silhouette holds its matching part. Give customers the corresponding ordered-layout drawing on the existing instruction sheet, explicitly locating the short partition.
openings.delta: Moves completeness checking ahead of insertion and uses spatial correspondence for both workshop selection and customer interpretation.
openings.prediction: Comparable mixed-layout orders show fewer selection corrections and shorter total preparation time; customers locate the short partition correctly more often.
openings.probe: Use spare board for templates and compare matched sample orders, including uncommon colors. Record selection, insertion, checking and packing separately, including template setup. Randomize ten participants between existing and order-specific diagrams. Check cost and remaining delivery time before adoption; evaluate all three success measures in the full pilot.
assumptions: Templates and existing-sheet printing fit the 500 initial and 0.40 recurring caps.
Check exterior color separately; preserve footprint, assortment, compartment counts and removable joints.

openings.claim: Insertion difficulty may depend on assembly order: an earlier partition could obstruct access or constrain a later slot. Inserting the short partition before intersecting partitions might avoid second attempts without dimensional changes.
openings.delta: Tests a reversible procedural cause; overlapping widths neither establish this explanation nor exclude dimensional problems.
openings.prediction: With the same parts and base, second-attempt frequency changes reproducibly with sequence. Persistent difficulty across sequences weakens the hypothesis.
openings.probe: Across spare-board samples and both workers, alternate short-partition-first and short-partition-last sequences, counterbalancing trial order. Record first-attempt success and assembly time; inspect for slot loosening from repeated use. If supported, test a numbered order-specific drawing with participants and include its cost before adoption.
assumptions: Counterbalancing and inspection adequately address learning and wear.
Instruction changes fit the cost caps and fixed schedule; product geometry, capacity, selected counts, color and removability remain intact.

critiques.assumption: A matching silhouette kit and ordered-layout drawing establish that the actual accepted order is complete and correctly represented.
critiques.limitation: If both inherit the same wrong layout mapping, they can agree while omitting a required partition. Neither such an error nor silhouette ambiguity is observed in the supplied case. A1's proposal does not explicitly require an order-source check independent of the spatial mapping; Z1 already proposes independent reconciliation.
critiques.opening: Retain spatial guidance but validate its mapping against the accepted order before reusing it, and reconcile each packed kit against that order.
critiques.comparison: Z1 supplies an independent completeness check but does not itself resolve customer placement; Z2 resolves placement only with correct contents and mapping. A1 combines spatial checking and interpretation. Adding Z1's independent reconciliation to A1 could interrupt shared mapping errors. The interaction is error containment across workshop and customer guidance; it fails if the checker merely copies the same mapping or its extra work defeats the time target.
critiques.probe: Proposed only: create sample kits containing correct parts, one omission, one substitution, and a deliberately wrong shared layout mapping. Compare A1 alone with A1 plus reconciliation against the accepted-order specification. Record detected discrepancies and all preparation/checking time. No physical tests have been performed.

openings.claim: Independent order reconciliation may make A1's shared spatial guidance robust to internally consistent mapping mistakes.
openings.delta: Validate each layout template against the accepted specification, then separately confirm packed component identities, counts and exterior color; retain the matching customer drawing.
openings.prediction: Compared with A1 alone, deliberately wrong shared mappings are caught more often. Compared with Z1 alone, the specific drawing may reduce customer placement errors. Both gains remain untested.
openings.probe: Reuse at most six sample sets for the discrepancy challenge across both workers. If feasible, use ten participants once each to compare verified kits with generic versus specific diagrams. Small trials assess mechanisms only; assess all three original success measures in the 60-unit pilot.
openings.fit: Conditional on measured feasibility within the original outcome and constraints.
assumptions: Accepted orders identify required components independently of the proposed mapping.
One bench, fifteen samples, 500 initial spending, 0.40 recurring increase and the fixed delivery date cover all work.
Footprint, assortment, removability, accepted counts and colors remain intact.
